name: Catalytic Hydrogenation of Alkenes
conditions: Ni (473-573 K) or Pt / Pd at room temp.
summary: Alkenes add H2 over finely divided Ni, Pt or Pd to give alkanes.
mechanism: H2 is adsorbed on the metal surface and both H atoms are delivered to the same face of the double bond (syn addition).
keyPoints: Exothermic; heat of hydrogenation measures alkene stability
Less substituted / less hindered alkene hydrogenates faster
Ni needs heat; Pt, Pd work at room temperature (Sabatier-Senderens)
whenUsed: Conversion of unsaturated hydrocarbons to saturated ones, hydrogenation of vegetable oils.
jeeTips: Heats of hydrogenation: trans-alkene < cis-alkene (more stable trans releases less heat). Benzene needs harsher conditions than alkenes. Syn addition on cyclic alkenes gives cis products, e.g. 1,2-dimethylcyclohexene gives cis-1,2-dimethylcyclohexane.

name: Addition of Halogens to Alkenes (Bromine Test)
summary: Br2 or Cl2 adds across a C=C bond to form vicinal dihalides; the red-brown colour of bromine is discharged.
mechanism: Alkene attacks Br2 to give a cyclic bromonium ion; Br- opens it from the back side, giving overall anti addition.
keyPoints: No rearrangement because of cyclic bromonium ion
I2 does not add (vicinal diiodide unstable)
whenUsed: Test for C=C / C≡C; synthesis of vicinal dihalides.
applications: Route to alkynes via double dehydrohalogenation
jeeTips: Cyclohexene + Br2 gives trans (anti) product; cis-but-2-ene gives racemic (2R,3R)/(2S,3S), trans-but-2-ene gives meso. Benzene does not decolourise bromine without FeBr3.

name: Halohydrin Formation (Br2 / H2O)
summary: Alkene with halogen in water gives a halohydrin: OH goes to the more substituted carbon, halogen to the less substituted.
mechanism: Bromonium ion forms; water (solvent, in large excess) attacks the more substituted carbon (greater positive character) from the back, then loses H+.
keyPoints: Markovnikov regiochemistry: OH on more substituted C
whenUsed: Making epoxides and glycols via bromohydrin.
jeeTips: Remember OH goes on the carbon bearing more alkyl groups; Br on the CH2. With Br2 in non-aqueous CCl4 you get the dibromide instead.

name: Alkynes by Double Dehydrohalogenation of Dihalides
summary: Vicinal or geminal dihalides lose two molecules of HX with strong base to give an alkyne.
mechanism: Two successive E2 eliminations; the vinyl halide intermediate needs a stronger base (NaNH2) for the second step.
keyPoints: Alc. KOH gives internal alkyne; NaNH2 / excess forces terminal alkyne isomerisation to acetylide
Route: alkene + Br2 then base = alkyne
whenUsed: Laboratory synthesis of alkynes from alkenes.
jeeTips: With NaNH2 a terminal alkyne is deprotonated; water work-up regenerates it. Count 2 equivalents of base (3 if terminal acetylide forms).

name: Preparation of Ethyne from Calcium Carbide
summary: Calcium carbide reacts with water to release ethyne; CaC2 itself is made from CaO and coke at 2273 K.
mechanism: The ionic C2^2- (acetylide) ion is a very strong base and is protonated twice by water.
keyPoints: Commercial gas has PH3 / H2S impurities (garlic smell)
Acetylide ion C2^2- is isoelectronic with N2
whenUsed: Oxy-acetylene welding, ethyne feedstock for other chemicals.
jeeTips: Mg2C3 + H2O gives propyne (CH3C#CH), a favourite trap. Al4C3 + H2O gives methane.

name: Alkylation of Terminal Alkynes (Acetylide + RX)
summary: Terminal alkyne is deprotonated by NaNH2 and the acetylide displaces halide from a primary alkyl halide, lengthening the chain.
mechanism: $\ce{RC#CH + NH2- -> RC#C- + NH3}$ then SN2 on RX.
keyPoints: Only 1° (or methyl) halides work; 2°/3° give elimination
Terminal alkyne pKa about 25, so NaNH2 (pKa NH3 about 38) is sufficient; NaOH is not
jeeTips: Use tert-alkyl halide and you get alkene, not alkyne. Alkyne + Na gives NaC#C and H2 gas.

name: Addition of HX to Alkynes
summary: Alkynes add one or two moles of HX following Markovnikov's rule, giving vinyl halides then geminal dihalides.
mechanism: Protonation gives a vinyl cation (more substituted), halide adds; second HX adds at the same carbon.
keyPoints: Markovnikov: both X on same C (gem-dihalide)
HC#CH + HCl (HgCl2, 333-343 K) gives vinyl chloride
jeeTips: Gem- not vicinal dihalide results; do not confuse with Br2 addition, which gives vicinal tetrabromides.

name: Pyrolysis (Cracking) of Alkanes
summary: Higher alkanes decompose at high temperature into mixtures of lower alkanes, alkenes and H2.
mechanism: Radical chain: C-C bond homolysis, then beta-scission of the radicals.
whenUsed: Refinery production of petrol and petrochemical alkenes.
jeeTips: Pyrolysis of alkanes proceeds by free-radicals; formation of alkenes + alkanes, not just fragments. Decane gives pentane + pentene as typical question.

name: Nitration of Nitrobenzene (m-Dinitrobenzene)
summary: NO2 deactivates the ring and directs the incoming NO2+ to the meta position; forcing conditions are required.
mechanism: NO2+ attacks the meta carbon because ortho/para attack puts positive charge next to the electron-withdrawing N+.
keyPoints: TNT-type polynitro compounds need more forcing steps
whenUsed: Preparation of m-dinitrobenzene, then m-nitroaniline via selective reduction (Na2S/(NH4)2S).
jeeTips: Meta directors: NO2, CN, CHO, COOH, SO3H, NR3+. Ring activation order and directing effect appear in assertion-reason items.

name: Electrophilic Substitution of Chlorobenzene
reagents: HNO3 / H2SO4 (or Cl2 / FeCl3, RCOCl / AlCl3)
summary: Halogen is deactivating by -I yet ortho/para-directing by +M, so chlorobenzene gives mainly para-substituted products.
mechanism: Resonance donation of lone pair stabilises ortho and para arenium ions; inductive withdrawal slows the ring overall.
keyPoints: Para major due to steric hindrance
whenUsed: Synthesis of p-substituted chlorobenzenes such as DDT.
jeeTips: p-isomer has higher m.p. than o-isomer (better crystal packing) and is separated by fractional crystallisation; o-isomer has higher dipole moment.

name: Synthesis of DDT (Chlorobenzene + Chloral)
summary: Two molecules of chlorobenzene condense with chloral under conc. H2SO4 to give DDT.
mechanism: Protonated chloral is the electrophile; EAS at the para position of chlorobenzene twice, with loss of water.
whenUsed: Historical insecticide; classic NCERT haloarene example.
jeeTips: Know the structure and that both rings have Cl at para positions. Chlorobenzene reacts at the para position.

name: Chlorination of Ethanol (Chloral and Chloral Hydrate)
summary: Excess chlorine oxidises ethanol to acetaldehyde and then chlorinates the alpha carbon, giving chloral; chloral forms a stable hydrate.
mechanism: Cl2 oxidises ethanol to CH3CHO, then successive enolisation/alpha-chlorination gives CCl3CHO.
keyPoints: Chloral hydrate CCl3CH(OH)2 is stable due to -I of CCl3
whenUsed: Precursor for DDT; chloroform from chloral.
jeeTips: Gem-diol is stable here because of electron-withdrawing CCl3 (a favourite stability question, with ninhydrin and ethyl glyoxylate).

name: Intermolecular Dehydration of Alcohols to Ethers
summary: Primary alcohols heated with conc. H2SO4 at 413 K (alcohol in excess) give symmetrical ethers; at 443 K the alkene forms instead.
mechanism: Alcohol is protonated; a second alcohol molecule attacks in an SN2 step, then loses H+.
keyPoints: Works only for primary alcohols (2°/3° give alkenes)
jeeTips: Temperature decides the product. For unsymmetrical ethers use Williamson synthesis rather than mixing two alcohols.

name: Ethylene Oxide + Grignard Reagent (Primary Alcohol, Two-Carbon Extension)
summary: Grignard reagents open the strained ethylene oxide ring at the CH2 carbon, giving a primary alcohol with two extra carbons after hydrolysis.
mechanism: R- attacks the epoxide carbon in an SN2 step, ring opens to alkoxide-MgX, which is hydrolysed.
keyPoints: Formaldehyde gives RCH2OH (1 carbon); ethylene oxide gives 2 carbons
Unsymmetrical epoxide: attack at less hindered C under basic conditions
whenUsed: Synthesis of primary alcohols with chain extension.
jeeTips: Count carbons: HCHO + RMgX = RCH2OH; ethylene oxide + RMgX = RCH2CH2OH; aldehyde gives 2°; ketone gives 3°.

name: Electrophilic Substitution of Anisole
reagents: Br2 / CH3COOH; or CH3COCl / anhyd. AlCl3
summary: The alkoxy group strongly activates the ring and directs ortho/para; bromination needs no Lewis acid.
mechanism: Resonance donation of oxygen lone pair stabilises o/p arenium ions.
keyPoints: OCH3 is a strong o/p activator
FC alkylation / acylation works (use more AlCl3)
HI cleavage gives phenol + CH3I only
jeeTips: Anisole + HI gives phenol + CH3I (O-aryl bond never breaks). Anisole is more reactive than benzene but less than phenol in some cases.

name: Reaction of Alcohols with Sodium (Acidity of Alcohols)
summary: Alcohols react with active metals (Na, K) to evolve H2 and give alkoxides, showing their weak acidity.
mechanism: O-H heterolysis assisted by electropositive metal.
keyPoints: Alcohols are weaker acids than water; phenol is stronger
whenUsed: Alkoxide formation for Williamson synthesis; test for OH group.

examples.note: Alkoxide is hydrolysed: alcohol is a weaker acid than water

jeeTips: Acidity order: water > ROH (1° > 2° > 3°) > alkynes > NH3 > alkanes. Alcohol does not react with NaOH, phenol does.

name: Dehydration of Glycerol to Acrolein
summary: Glycerol on heating with a dehydrating agent such as KHSO4 loses two molecules of water to give acrolein, a pungent-smelling aldehyde used to identify fats and glycerol.
mechanism: First dehydration gives an enol that tautomerises to 3-hydroxypropanal, which loses a second H2O.
keyPoints: Acrolein test for glycerol / fats (acrid smell)
whenUsed: Detection of glycerol; lab preparation of acrolein.
jeeTips: HBr adds to acrolein at the beta-carbon (conjugate addition) giving 3-bromopropanal, anti-Markovnikov looking.

name: Nitration of Glycerol (Nitroglycerine, Dynamite)
summary: All three OH groups of glycerol are esterified by the nitrating mixture, giving an explosive nitrate ester.
mechanism: Acid-catalysed esterification with nitric acid (O-nitration).
keyPoints: It is a nitrate ester (not nitro compound)
jeeTips: Nitrate ester (R-O-NO2) vs nitro compound (R-NO2) distinction is tested.

name: Synthesis of Aspirin (Acetylation of Salicylic Acid)
summary: Phenolic OH of salicylic acid is acetylated by acetic anhydride to give aspirin, an analgesic, antipyretic and anti-platelet drug.
mechanism: Nucleophilic acyl substitution of phenolic oxygen on the anhydride.
keyPoints: Aspirin hydrolyses back to salicylic acid (vinegar smell)
Methyl salicylate (oil of wintergreen) from esterification of COOH with CH3OH
jeeTips: FeCl3 test: salicylic acid gives violet colour; pure aspirin does not (no free phenolic OH).

name: Benzaldehyde from Benzal Chloride (Side-Chain Chlorination then Hydrolysis)
summary: Toluene is chlorinated at the methyl group (Cl2, hv) to benzal chloride, which on hydrolysis gives benzaldehyde.
mechanism: Gem-dihalide hydrolyses to gem-diol (hydrate) which loses H2O to the aldehyde.
keyPoints: Benzotrichloride C6H5CCl3 hydrolyses to benzoic acid
Gem-diols are unstable and lose water
jeeTips: Number of Cl on the benzylic carbon decides: 1 Cl gives alcohol, 2 Cl gives aldehyde, 3 Cl gives acid.

name: Ketones by Dry Distillation of Calcium Salts of Acids
summary: Heating calcium salt of a carboxylic acid gives a ketone; with calcium formate as co-reactant an aldehyde is obtained.
mechanism: Thermal decarboxylative coupling of the two acyl groups.
keyPoints: Ca formate + Ca acetate gives CH3CHO
Ca benzoate + Ca formate gives benzaldehyde
whenUsed: Lab preparation of ketones and aldehydes.
jeeTips: Mixed salts give three products (statistical); pairing with formate favours aldehydes. Count C atoms carefully.

name: Esters + Grignard Reagent (Tertiary Alcohols)
summary: Esters react with two equivalents of RMgX; the ketone formed is more reactive than ester so a tertiary alcohol with two identical R groups results.
mechanism: First addition-elimination gives ketone, second addition gives alkoxide.
keyPoints: Two identical R groups from Grignard
Acid chlorides also give 3° alcohols (excess RMgX)
jeeTips: Formate esters give secondary; all others tertiary. Reaction with RCN stops at ketone (after hydrolysis).

name: Amides from Carboxylic Acids (Ammonium Salt Pyrolysis) and Amide Hydrolysis
summary: Carboxylic acid with ammonia gives ammonium salt which on heating dehydrates to the amide; amides hydrolyse back with acid or alkali.
mechanism: Acid-base reaction gives RCOO- NH4+, then thermal nucleophilic acyl substitution loses H2O.
keyPoints: Hydrolysis: H3O+ gives acid + NH4+; NaOH gives carboxylate + NH3
whenUsed: Preparation of amides, intermediate for Hofmann bromamide.
jeeTips: Amide is much less basic than amine; N lone pair delocalised onto C=O. Hydrolysis rate order: acid chloride > anhydride > ester > amide.

name: Preparation of Carboxylic Acid Anhydrides
summary: Dehydration of carboxylic acids (or acid chloride + carboxylate) gives anhydrides.
mechanism: Nucleophilic acyl substitution of RCOCl by RCOO-.
keyPoints: Succinic and phthalic acids cyclise on heating
Acid chloride + sodium carboxylate is general route
whenUsed: Making acylating agents; phthalic anhydride from phthalic acid.
jeeTips: Mixed anhydride from CH3COCl + HCOONa is unstable. 1,4- and 1,5-dicarboxylic acids form 5/6-membered cyclic anhydrides.

name: Reaction of Aldehydes and Ketones with PCl5
summary: The carbonyl O is replaced by two Cl atoms, giving geminal dichlorides.
mechanism: Oxygen attacks P, chloride adds to C+; second Cl- displaces OPCl4-.
jeeTips: Compare: alcohol + PCl5 gives RCl + POCl3 + HCl; acid + PCl5 gives acid chloride.

name: Formaldehyde: Polymerisation and Urotropine Formation
summary: Formaldehyde with ammonia gives urotropine; on its own it polymerises to trioxane or paraformaldehyde. 40% aqueous HCHO is formalin.
mechanism: Repeated addition of NH3 to C=O then condensation forms the cage compound.
jeeTips: Formalin is a 40% solution; HCHO + NH3 does NOT give an imine because it condenses further.

name: Reduction of Nitriles and Amides to Amines
summary: Nitriles, amides and isonitriles are reduced to amines; nitriles/amides keep the same carbon count, isonitriles give N-methylamines.
mechanism: Successive hydride additions to the C#N or C=O carbon then protonation.
keyPoints: Nitrile to 1° amine (carbon count same as nitrile)
Hofmann bromamide, in contrast, removes one carbon
whenUsed: Preparing 1° amines with ascending carbon series (RX to RCN to RCH2NH2).
jeeTips: RCN / RCONH2 -> amine retains carbons, Hofmann gives one carbon less. LiAlH4 reduces amide to amine, but NaBH4 doesn't.

name: Haloalkanes with Aqueous vs Alcoholic KOH (Substitution vs Elimination)
summary: In aqueous KOH, OH- is a nucleophile and gives an alcohol; in alcoholic KOH, the stronger base RO-/OH- favours E2 elimination to alkene.
mechanism: Aq: SN2 / SN1; Alc: E2 (anti-periplanar H).
keyPoints: Tertiary halides eliminate even in aq. KOH
whenUsed: Choosing between alcohol and alkene synthesis.
jeeTips: Aq. KOH has OH- but is also solvated by water so less basic; alcoholic KOH contains RO- (stronger base).

name: Basicity of Amines: Salt Formation and Liberation
summary: Amines are basic and form water-soluble ammonium salts with mineral acids; strong base regenerates the free amine.
mechanism: Lone pair on N accepts H+.
keyPoints: Basic order in aqueous medium (alkylamines): 2° > 3° > 1° (R = CH3: 2° > 1° > 3°; R = C2H5: 2° > 3° > 1°)
Aniline is weaker base than NH3 (lone pair delocalised)
Salts with chloroplatinic acid for estimation of N
whenUsed: Separation of amines from neutral compounds; purification.

examples.eq: CH3NH3+ Cl- + NaOH -> CH3NH2 + NaCl + H2O

jeeTips: Gas-phase order is 3° > 2° > 1° > NH3; aqueous order differs because of solvation. EWG on aniline decreases basicity, EDG increases it.

name: Mutarotation of Glucose
summary: Anomers of glucose interconvert via the open-chain aldehyde form in water, so the specific rotation changes from +111 or +19.2 to +52.5 degrees.
mechanism: Ring opens via hemiacetal, rotates about C1-C2, recloses to the other anomer.
keyPoints: Anomers differ only at C-1 (anomeric carbon)
whenUsed: Explains why glucose lacks some typical aldehyde reactions (NaHSO3, Schiff).
jeeTips: Anomers are diastereomers (epimers at C-1), not enantiomers. Glucose does not give Schiff's test or NaHSO3 addition.

name: Hydrolysis of Maltose, Lactose and Starch
summary: Maltose gives two glucose units; lactose gives glucose + galactose; starch gives maltose and then glucose.
mechanism: Acid or enzymatic cleavage of glycosidic (acetal) bonds.
jeeTips: Reducing vs non-reducing: only sucrose among the common disaccharides is non-reducing (no free anomeric OH).

name: Polystyrene (Addition Polymerisation of Styrene)
summary: Styrene polymerises by free-radical addition to a transparent thermoplastic.
mechanism: Initiation, propagation, termination radical chain.
jeeTips: Know the monomer: phenylethene. Polystyrene is an addition polymer with no heteroatom.

name: PMMA (Perspex / Plexiglass)
summary: Methyl methacrylate undergoes radical addition polymerisation to give transparent plastic.
mechanism: Radical chain, tertiary radical stabilised by ester.

examples.note: Acetone cyanohydrin, starting point for the monomer

jeeTips: Monomer is methyl 2-methylpropenoate. Tertiary carbon on chain.

name: Polyacrylonitrile (Orlon / Acrilan)
summary: Acrylonitrile polymerises through free-radical addition to a fibre used as artificial wool.
mechanism: Radical chain.
jeeTips: Monomer is vinyl cyanide (propenenitrile). Don't confuse with nylon (condensation).

name: PHBV (Poly-beta-hydroxybutyrate-co-beta-hydroxyvalerate)
summary: Condensation copolymerisation of 3-hydroxybutanoic acid and 3-hydroxypentanoic acid gives a biodegradable polyester.
mechanism: Intermolecular esterification between OH and COOH.
jeeTips: Monomers: 3-hydroxybutanoic and 3-hydroxypentanoic acids; know that it is biodegradable.

name: Hydroboration-Oxidation of Alkynes
summary: Terminal alkynes give aldehydes (anti-Markovnikov hydration) via bulky borane then H2O2/NaOH; internal alkynes give ketones.
mechanism: Syn addition of H and B (B on terminal C); enol formed on oxidation tautomerises to aldehyde.
jeeTips: HgSO4 route: ketone; borane route: aldehyde. Syn addition of H-B.

name: Pinacol Coupling of Ketones (Mg-Hg / Mg)
summary: Bimolecular reduction of ketones/aldehydes by Mg amalgam gives vicinal diols (pinacols).
mechanism: Single electron transfer forms ketyl radical anions which dimerise (C-C bond), hydrolysis gives diol.
whenUsed: Making vicinal diols; sets up pinacol rearrangement questions.
jeeTips: Pair with pinacol-pinacolone rearrangement: a two-step ketone to rearranged ketone question.

name: Acyloin Condensation
summary: Esters are reductively coupled by sodium metal to alpha-hydroxy ketones (acyloins); intramolecular version closes rings.
mechanism: Radical anion dimerisation, loss of alkoxide gives 1,2-diketone, further reduction gives ene-diolate then acyloin.
keyPoints: Intramolecular: ring formation from diesters (C5 and up)
whenUsed: Forming alpha-hydroxy ketones and medium rings.
jeeTips: Dry, aprotic solvent essential. Alcohol present gives reduction rather than coupling.

name: Swern Oxidation
summary: Primary alcohols give aldehydes and secondary alcohols give ketones under mild, over-oxidation-free conditions using activated DMSO.
mechanism: DMSO + oxalyl chloride gives chlorodimethylsulfonium; alcohol adds, base removes alpha-H, ylide collapses to C=O + Me2S.
jeeTips: Know that Swern stops at the aldehyde, like PCC. Tertiary alcohols are untouched.

name: Ritter Reaction
summary: A carbocation (from tertiary alcohol or alkene) is trapped by a nitrile N to give an N-alkyl amide after water work-up.
mechanism: Carbocation + RC#N gives nitrilium ion; water adds, tautomerises to amide.
jeeTips: Carbocation chemistry in strongly acidic, non-aqueous nitrile solvent. Rearrangements can occur.

name: Tiffeneau-Demjanov Ring Expansion
summary: 1-Aminomethylcycloalkanol with HNO2 gives diazonium which loses N2 with ring expansion by one carbon.
mechanism: Diazonium leaves, alkyl shift to the electron-deficient CH2, then proton loss gives ketone.
keyPoints: Combines cyanohydrin, reduction and diazotisation of 1deg amine
jeeTips: Aliphatic primary amine + HNO2 gives N2 and cation, not stable diazonium.

name: Carbocation Rearrangement in Alcohol Dehydration (Wagner-Meerwein)
summary: A secondary carbocation shifts a methyl (or hydride) group to give a more stable tertiary cation, which loses H+ to the most substituted alkene.
mechanism: Protonation, loss of water, 1,2-methyl shift, E1.
keyPoints: Shifts: H or CH3 to cationic centre
Seen with neopentyl-type and neighbouring tertiary carbons
jeeTips: Ask yourself first: is there a more stable cation obtainable by a 1,2-shift? Then apply Saytzeff.

name: Intramolecular Aldol Condensation (Cyclisation of Diketones)
summary: 1,4- and 1,5-diketones cyclise via intramolecular aldol to give 5- or 6-membered cyclic enones.
mechanism: Enolate of one C=O attacks the other; dehydration gives conjugated enone.
jeeTips: Count rings: 3- and 4-membered rings do not form; pick the ring size 5/6.

name: Intramolecular Cannizzaro Reaction (Glyoxal, Phthalaldehyde)
summary: Dialdehydes lacking alpha-H undergo internal hydride transfer to give a hydroxy-acid salt.
mechanism: Hydroxide adds to one CHO, hydride shifts to adjacent CHO within the same molecule.
jeeTips: One molecule gives both acid and alcohol; no second molecule required.

name: Benzidine Rearrangement
summary: Hydrazobenzene rearranges in acid to benzidine (4,4'-diaminobiphenyl) via a [5,5]-type shift.
mechanism: Diprotonation then concerted para-para bond formation with N-N cleavage.
keyPoints: Nitrobenzene to azobenzene to hydrazobenzene to benzidine (reduction route)
jeeTips: Nitrobenzene + Zn/NaOH goes to hydrazobenzene; then acid gives benzidine.

name: Oxidative Cleavage of 1,2-Diols (HIO4 / Pb(OAc)4)
summary: Periodic acid or lead tetraacetate cleaves vicinal diols (and alpha-hydroxy carbonyls) at the C-C bond giving aldehydes/ketones.
mechanism: A cyclic periodate ester forms and fragments.
jeeTips: Count moles of HIO4 consumed: one per C-C bond broken. Cyclic cis-diols cleave faster.

name: Lobry de Bruyn-van Ekenstein Transformation (Glucose-Fructose-Mannose)
productName: Mixture of glucose, mannose and fructose
summary: In dilute alkali an aldose tautomerises through an enediol to its C-2 epimer and the isomeric ketose.
mechanism: Base removes alpha-H, enediol formed, reprotonation either face.
keyPoints: Glucose and mannose are C-2 epimers
Explains why fructose gives Tollens' and Fehling's positive
whenUsed: Why ketoses behave as reducing sugars.
jeeTips: Fructose is a ketose but gives Tollens test due to this isomerisation.

name: Wohl Degradation of Aldoses
summary: An aldose is shortened by one carbon: oxime, acetylation/dehydration to cyanide, then loss of HCN.
mechanism: Oxime dehydrates to cyanohydrin acetate, base removes HCN regenerating CHO.
jeeTips: Opposite of Kiliani-Fischer (ascending). Glucose to arabinose.

name: Conjugate Addition of Gilman Reagent to Enones
summary: Lithium dialkylcuprates add to alpha,beta-unsaturated carbonyls at the beta carbon (1,4-addition), whereas Grignards/RLi favour 1,2-addition.
mechanism: R transfers from Cu to beta carbon giving enolate; protonation gives saturated ketone.
jeeTips: Choose the reagent by regiochemistry: R2CuLi gives conjugate addition product, RMgX gives allylic alcohol.

name: Birch Reduction of Substituted Benzenes (EDG vs EWG)
summary: EDG (OCH3, CH3) remain on the double bond (sp2 carbon) while EWG (COOH) end up on an sp3 carbon in the 1,4-diene.
mechanism: Electron transfer gives radical anion, protonation and repeat; protonation occurs at positions that avoid placing negative charge next to EDG.
jeeTips: Alkyl/alkoxy stays on double bond; COOH on saturated C. Extends the benzene Birch reaction.
